article.title: Why Calibration Matters When a Model Score Is Used as a Probability
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: A model can rank customers well and still produce unreliable probabilities. This distinction matters whenever a score is used not only to order customers but also to estimate expected conversions, revenue, risk, or economic value. Discrimination asks whether positive cases tend to receive higher scores than negative cases. Metrics such as AUC focus on ranking. Calibration asks a different question: among cases assigned a predicted probability near 20 percent, does the event occur about 20 percent of the time? A model can have strong AUC and poor calibration. This often happens when class weights, oversampling, undersampling, or certain algorithms change the relationship between raw scores and real-world event rates. In highly imbalanced problems, the issue can be especially important. Suppose a targeting model assigns 0.30 to a group of customers. If the true conversion rate is only 0.03, treating 0.30 as a literal probability will greatly overestimate expected value. Ranking may still be useful if higher scores correspond to higher conversion rates, but economic calculations will be wrong. Calibration should be evaluated on data that represents the deployment population and time period. Reliability diagrams or calibration curves compare predicted probabilities with observed event rates across bins. Brier score summarizes squared probability error, while log loss provides another probability-sensitive metric. No single metric tells the entire story. Calibration can vary by segment. A model may be well calibrated overall while overpredicting for one channel and underpredicting for another. Segment checks are important when decisions or costs differ across groups. Calibration can also drift over time even when ranking remains stable. A change in the base event rate can shift the mapping from score to probability. This is why monitoring only AUC may miss a serious problem for value estimation. Post-hoc calibration methods such as Platt scaling or isotonic regression can improve probability estimates when they are fitted on appropriate validation data. Cross-validation or a separate calibration set helps reduce overfitting. Calibration does not repair every model problem. If feature relationships have changed substantially or data quality is broken, recalibrating a bad model can create false confidence. Diagnosis should come first. Decision thresholds should also reflect the use case. If the model is used only to choose the top 100,000 customers, ranking quality may dominate. If the score is multiplied by margin to estimate expected profit, probability accuracy becomes much more important. Treatment-effect models add another complication because the quantity of interest may be an incremental probability rather than an ordinary outcome probability. Those estimates require their own validation logic. The practical lesson is to ask what the score means operationally. A number between zero and one is not automatically a trustworthy probability. If business decisions interpret it as one, calibration must be measured, monitored, and maintained.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it.
